pdf.title: NCERT Class 9 Contemporary India–I · Chapter 5: Natural Vegetation and Wildlife

meta.subject: Geography
meta.title: Natural Vegetation and Wildlife
meta.intro: The meaning and factors of natural vegetation, major forest types in India, biodiversity, wildlife distribution, threats and conservation measures.

objectives: Explain natural vegetation and wildlife using geographical concepts and Indian examples.
Identify the important terms, patterns, processes and locations in this chapter.
Interpret maps, tables and geographical evidence.
Connect the chapter with human life, environment and regional development.

blocks.text: Natural vegetation refers to plant communities that grow naturally without direct human assistance and remain largely undisturbed over a long period. A plant community that has grown naturally in an area is often described as virgin vegetation.

Climate is the most important broad control of vegetation. Temperature, photoperiod and precipitation determine the length of the growing season and the availability of moisture. Soil, slope and altitude also influence plant growth.
The plant life occurring naturally in a particular region or period.
The animal life occurring naturally in a particular region or period.
Human activities such as agriculture, settlement, mining, grazing, logging and infrastructure development modify natural vegetation and habitats.

Tropical evergreen forests occur in areas of very high rainfall and warm temperatures throughout the year. Trees remain green because different species shed leaves at different times. These forests are dense, multi-layered and rich in biodiversity.
Evergreen forests occur in the Western Ghats, parts of northeastern India and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Important trees include ebony, mahogany, rosewood and rubber.

Tropical deciduous forests are also called monsoon forests. Trees shed leaves during the dry season to reduce water loss. They are widespread across much of India and are divided into moist and dry deciduous types.
Teak, sal, shisham, sandalwood, khair and bamboo are associated with different deciduous forest regions. The exact composition varies with rainfall and soil.

Tropical thorn forests and scrub occur in regions receiving low rainfall, including parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat and the rain-shadow interiors. Plants have small leaves, thorns, deep roots and other adaptations to conserve water.

Montane forests change with altitude. Lower slopes may support broad-leaved forests; higher elevations support temperate conifers such as pine, deodar, silver fir and spruce. Alpine vegetation, including grasses and shrubs, occurs near the snowline.

Mangrove or tidal forests grow in saline coastal swamps, estuaries and deltas. Their roots are adapted to waterlogged and oxygen-poor soils. The Sundarbans are a major mangrove region; mangroves also occur in the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.
India has varied wildlife because its climates, landforms and vegetation types create many habitats. Wildlife includes mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, insects and other organisms.

Large mammals include the elephant, tiger, lion, rhinoceros, snow leopard and several deer species. Different species are adapted to forests, grasslands, mountains, wetlands, deserts and coastal ecosystems.
Biodiversity supports food webs, pollination, soil formation, nutrient cycling, water regulation and ecological stability. It also has cultural, scientific, recreational and livelihood value.
Habitat fragmentation, deforestation, poaching, pollution, invasive species and climate change threaten wildlife. A species may become endangered when its population and habitat decline severely.

In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitats through national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves and biosphere reserves. Ex-situ measures include zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and captive breeding programmes.

The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 provides a legal framework for wildlife protection in India. Project Tiger, launched in 1973, supports tiger conservation and habitat protection. Project Elephant was launched in 1992.

Community participation is essential. Joint Forest Management, local stewardship, sacred groves and sustainable use practices can support conservation when local communities have meaningful roles and benefits.

blocks.title: Key distinction
blocks.text: A national park generally provides stronger protection to an ecosystem; a wildlife sanctuary focuses on protecting wildlife and may allow certain regulated activities under law.
